title: Rome falls (410)
hook: the city is sacked, and Augustine writes City of God: two cities, two loves

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ostia, where Augustine and Monica talked at a window. Your line was at the window.

The news crosses the sea, and it's hard to believe. Rome has been sacked. An army of Goths has broken into the city and plundered it. People who fled are arriving. And some say out loud what they're thinking: this happened because Rome turned from its old gods to the Christian one. Across the water in Africa, Augustine is now a bishop. He hears the charge, picks up his pen to answer it, and the answer grows into a very long book.
screen: `THE OLD GODS, OR THE NEW ONE?`

segments.voice: The book is The City of God. Augustine starts with the charge itself. During the sack, he points out, the invaders spared people who fled into the churches of the apostles, and some of those spared are now the ones blaming Christ. Then he goes much further than a reply. There are two cities mixed together in this world, he says. Not two places. Two loves. The Psalms sing of one, in the King James words: "Glorious things are spoken of thee, O city of God." Beside it Augustine sets the earthly city. Then comes the line that holds the whole book together. Two loves have made two cities. Love of self, reaching even to contempt of God, made the earthly city. Love of God, reaching even to contempt of self, made the heavenly one. That changes the question. For Augustine, Rome was never the city of God, not even a Christian Rome. No empire is. The two cities run through every street and every church, tangled together until the end. So when Rome falls, he tells his readers, they may grieve, but their hope was not built on its walls. The letter to the Hebrews had said it: "For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come." That's no excuse to stop caring. The heavenly city, Augustine says, while on pilgrimage here, makes use of the earthly city's peace and seeks it, since its people share that life too. But every city, party and institution faces the same question: what does it love? And the question runs through each person, too.
screen: `NO EMPIRE IS THE CITY OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Think of the places your days go into: your work, your home, a group you belong to, the screen in your pocket. Pick one, and ask Augustine's question of it quietly: what does it love, and what am I adding to it, love that curls inward or love that turns outward? Don't grade yourself; just look, and if you pray, offer that place to God.
Rome falls. The sack of the city that set Augustine writing The City of God: two cities, made by two loves, mixed until the end.
Your line: two cities, two loves. The walls can fall; the question stays. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Augustine's City of God is read and taught by Christians of different churches, especially when they think about faith and public life; his image of two cities and two loves is often cited in that conversation.

fork.setup: you're a bishop. people who fled Rome are arriving, and some say the city fell because it abandoned its old gods. what do you do?
options: say nothing: the talk will pass.
answer the charge, then write about two cities and two loves.

fork.reveal: Augustine answered, and kept going. his reply became The City of God: no empire is God's city; two loves build two cities.

chat.says: When Rome was sacked, did Augustine think God had abandoned the Christians?
options: No. He said no empire is the city of God; their hope wasn't built on Rome's walls.
Yes. He said Rome fell because Christians had stopped praying for the empire.
He agreed the old gods were angry, and urged Christians to make peace with them.
chat.meaning: For Augustine, two loves make two cities, and no empire is the city of God. Believers could grieve Rome without losing their hope.

notes: No year is spoken (the index title carries 410). The Goths are named; Alaric is not. Confirm 'people who fled are arriving with nothing' (refugees to Africa are attested in Augustine's sermons and letters, not cited here).
City of God 1.1 and 1.7: the barbarians spared those who fled to the basilicas of the apostles, including some now blaming Christ. Paraphrased; confirm.
City of God 14.28: 'two loves have formed two cities' paraphrased (Dods 1871 is not on the public-domain list used here).
City of God 19.17: the heavenly city on pilgrimage makes use of the earthly peace. Confirm paraphrase.
Not stated: how long Augustine took or how many books the work has (claims rule). 'A very long book' is a soft description; confirm.
